protein-calculator.assumptionNote: Factors follow ISSN sport-nutrition ranges for healthy adults. Kidney disease needs medical limits.
benefits: Ends the 'am I eating enough protein?' guessing.
Per-meal splits make the target actually cookable.
Protects muscle during fat loss - the main job of protein.
Based on sport-nutrition ranges, not influencer claims.

faqs.a: Healthy kidneys handle up to ~2.5-3 g/kg fine. Beyond ~2.2 g/kg there is just no extra muscle benefit - the surplus becomes expensive calories.
faqs.q: Can I eat too much protein?

faqs.a: Yes with variety. Combine legumes, grains, soy, and nuts across the day; soy and quinoa are complete proteins on their own. You may need slightly more total grams since plant protein digests a bit less completely.
The 'anabolic window' is wider than claimed - total daily protein matters far more than timing. Eating within a few hours of training is plenty.
faqs.q: Do I need protein right after training?

faqs.a: A convenience, not a requirement. One scoop (~25 g) helps when whole food is impractical. It counts exactly like food protein.
Yes - about 1.2-1.6 g/kg. Aging muscles resist growth signals, so older adults need more protein per meal (~40 g) to trigger the same response.
faqs.q: Should older adults eat more protein?

faqs.a: Yes: it is the most filling macro, costs energy to digest (~20-30% of its calories), and protects muscle in a deficit - which keeps metabolism higher.

protein-calculator.formula:
Daily protein (g) = weight (kg) x factor

Factors:
Sedentary: 1.2
Lightly active: 1.4
Active: 1.6
Building muscle: 1.8
Dieting / athlete: 2.0

Per meal = daily / meals

Example: 70 kg, active
= 70 x 1.6 = 112 g/day
Per meal (3): 112 / 3 = 37.3 g
howTo: Enter your body weight in kg.
Pick the activity level closest to your life.
Your daily grams appear instantly, with 3-meal and 4-meal splits.
Build each meal around a palm-sized protein portion.
Recalculate if your weight changes by 5 kg or your training changes.
keyFacts: Protein needs scale with body weight: 1.2-2.2 g per kg per day.
Sedentary: ~1.2 g/kg. Active: ~1.6 g/kg. Building muscle or dieting: 1.8-2.0 g/kg.
Spread protein across 3-4 meals - the body uses ~30-50 g per meal best.
Good sources: eggs (~6 g each), chicken breast (~31 g per 100 g), lentils (~9 g per 100 g cooked), Greek yogurt (~10 g per 100 g).
Kidneys handle high protein fine in healthy people - the risk myth comes from existing kidney disease.

limitations: Uses total body weight - very overweight people should use lean mass or target weight.
Factors are ranges; individual needs vary with age and training.
Does not assess protein quality - vary your sources.
People with kidney disease need a doctor's limits, not this calculator.

protein-calculator.quickAnswer: Multiply body weight by 1.2-2.0 g/kg depending on activity. A 70 kg active person needs about 112 g per day (70 x 1.6) - roughly 37 g across 3 meals. Dieters and athletes go higher (2.0 g/kg); sedentary people need less (1.2 g/kg).
protein-calculator.tagline: Your daily protein target from body weight and activity - with per-meal splits.
protein-calculator.workedExample:
You weigh 70 kg and train regularly (active):
1. Pick the factor: active = 1.6 g/kg.
2. Multiply: 70 x 1.6 = 112 g per day.
3. Split over 3 meals: 112 / 3 = 37.3 g per meal.
4. Split over 4 meals: 112 / 4 = 28 g per meal.
5. In food terms: about 4 eggs (24 g) + 150 g chicken breast (~46 g) + 200 g Greek yogurt (~20 g) + lentils and grains for the rest.
